lines.text: Vitamin C and iodine are two of many. Each vitamin and each mineral
has its own job, its own food sources, and its own set of symptoms
when the body runs short. Together they are what keep the body's
defences and daily processes working.
Fig. 3.5 on the next page sets out the main ones. Read it carefully —
you will be using it again in the exercises at the end of the chapter.
ACTIVITY
Activity 3.4 — A survey in your neighbourhood
Carry out this activity under your teacher's guidance.
Study Fig. 3.5 until you know the symptoms listed in the last column.
Talk to people in your neighbourhood — with their permission, and
politely. Ask whether they have noticed any of these symptoms in
themselves or their family: trouble seeing in dim light, bleeding gums,
weakness and breathlessness, aching or bending bones.
Where someone reports a symptom, ask — again, politely — what they
usually eat. Look for a food group that is largely missing.
Correlate the two. Which deficiency would fit the symptoms and the
diet together?
Suggest which foods, easily available and affordable locally, could help.
Always end by suggesting they see a doctor.
A warning that matters. You are not diagnosing anyone. A symptom can
have many causes, and only a doctor can test and treat. Your job here is
to practise linking evidence to explanation — and then to hand the matter
to someone qualified.
